title: Office Purchasing Pilot
summary: Threadline Delivery built a single-manager purchasing pilot for one office. Staff created purchase requests and managers approved a specific request revision.
problem: Office staff previously emailed item lists to their manager. When a quantity changed, an old approval could remain attached to an outdated list. The client needed one place to see the requested items, the current total, and the revision that a manager had actually approved. The pilot covered office supplies only; it did not place orders or move money.
users: The requester created and amended a request. The assigned office manager reviewed it. An office administrator inspected the event history and recorded a manual purchase reference after approval. The same person could not submit and approve the same request. There was one office and one approval stage; there was no finance reviewer or branch hierarchy.
workflow: A request began as a draft with item descriptions, quantities, unit prices, and a reason. Submit created an immutable revision and moved it to awaiting manager review. The manager approved or rejected that revision. Editing submitted quantities or prices created another revision and returned the request to review. The earlier decision remained in the history but no longer authorized the edited request.
constraints: The pilot used Next.js, PostgreSQL, and the client's existing employee sign-in. A server-side transition checked the requester, manager assignment, current state, and expected revision. The pilot did not include amount-based routing, offline drafts, supplier onboarding, finance approval, or purchase-order generation. These exclusions were written before implementation so that a small pilot would not be mistaken for a complete procurement platform.
decision: Approval was bound to a request revision rather than a mutable request row. A transaction inserted the decision and changed state only when the submitted revision still matched the manager's screen. A stale manager screen received a conflict and had to reload. The design deliberately kept rejected and superseded revisions rather than overwriting their item lists.
detail: The tables were purchase_request, request_revision, approval_decision, and request_event. Each revision kept a calculated total in integer VND. The server recalculated it from submitted line items rather than trusting a browser total. Request events identified the actor, revision, old state, new state, and server timestamp. The database transaction prevented a state update from succeeding without its corresponding decision record.
example: Request PO-014 asked for four chairs. A manager opened revision 2, then the requester increased the quantity to six, creating revision 3. Approving revision 2 returned a revision conflict. The manager reloaded and approved revision 3. The history showed both the amendment and the later approval, making it possible for the administrator to explain which list was authorized.
test: Acceptance checks exercised manager approval, self-approval rejection, an edit after approval, and a stale manager screen. The approved request could not remain approved after its quantity changed. These were scripted functional checks using fictional employee accounts and a single office. No test exercised multiple branches or a second finance decision, because those behaviors had not been built.
result: The one-office pilot was accepted for request submission, single-manager review, revision checks, and inspection of request events. No finance approval stage was delivered.
incident: During acceptance testing, the team found that an early screen showed the previous approval next to an amended item list. Release was held until the screen labelled that decision as superseded and the server enforced revision matching. The corrected pilot was accepted; the initial screen defect should remain in the delivery record rather than being described as a feature that was always correct.
lesson: An approval must identify the exact request revision it authorizes. A later edit requires a new decision; preserving an old decision is not permission to reuse it.
gap: Approval-time savings, multi-branch behavior, and finance routing were not measured or implemented in this pilot. The client accepted a narrow workflow, not a general purchasing platform.
handover: The handover included the transition checklist, revision-conflict example, database relationship sketch, and acceptance notes. An engineer can use these records to understand the design, but this document pack contains no application source code or drop-in library. Any reuse still requires implementation, integration with current sign-in, and tests against the new client's approval rules.

title: Expense Reimbursement Portal
status: Delivered internal pilot after retry defect repair
summary: Threadline Delivery built an expense-claim portal. Retry testing exposed duplicate claim creation, and a stable operation key plus a database constraint prevented the same operation from creating another claim.
problem: Consultants submitted receipt details from mobile browsers. A slow response made it unclear whether the server had received a claim, so users pressed Send again or retried after reconnecting. An early prototype treated each HTTP request as a new claim. The business needed reliable recording of a claim before any separate human reimbursement process could begin.
users: An employee entered the amount, reason, and receipt reference. A reviewer checked a claim and marked it ready for the payroll team's separate process. A support operator investigated unclear submissions using an operation identifier. The portal did not connect to a bank, initiate a payment, or decide whether an expense met a tax rule. Those were outside the software pilot.
workflow: The browser created a submission identifier when the employee began sending a completed claim. The identifier stayed the same while retrying that operation. If the first attempt committed but its response was lost, a retry returned the recorded claim instead of inserting another. An intentional second claim used a new identifier, even if its amount happened to be the same.
constraints: The team used a browser form, a server API, and PostgreSQL. Disabling the Send button was helpful feedback but could not enforce uniqueness across reconnects, multiple browser events, or concurrent requests. The requirement concerned duplicate claim records for the same operation, not detection of a person intentionally submitting a receipt twice with different identifiers. No offline queue was included.
decision: The stable operation key was scoped to the submitting employee. A unique database constraint on employee_id and operation_key serialized duplicate creation attempts. The server stored a normalized payload fingerprint with the claim. Reusing a key with a different payload returned a conflict instead of silently attaching changed receipt details to the first claim.
detail: Claim creation ran inside a database transaction. A repeated matching operation loaded the existing claim and returned its identifier and current status. Concurrent requests competed on the unique constraint, so the loser read the winner's committed record. The client retained the key across a timeout and cleared it only after confirmation or an explicit decision to start a different submission.
example: Employee E-18 submitted claim EXP-042. The database committed, but a simulated network interruption hid the response. The browser retried with the same operation key and identical receipt details. The server returned EXP-042. A later attempt that changed the amount while keeping that key was rejected as a conflicting operation and required the user to review the form.
test: Regression checks covered a response lost after commit, two simultaneous matching submissions, and the same key with a changed payload. In the controlled checks, matching retries returned one claim identifier and a changed payload produced a conflict. The checks used a synthetic network failure and test accounts. They did not establish reliability under real production traffic or indefinite retry retention.
result: After the repair, controlled lost-response and concurrent-retry checks produced one claim record per matching operation. A changed payload with the same operation key was rejected.
incident: The prototype created two claim records when a response was lost and the browser repeated the submission. The team caught this in staging before the pilot handover. No payment was executed by the portal, and the incident record does not establish any duplicate reimbursement. The correction addressed record creation, not every possible duplicate business claim.
lesson: Keep one stable operation key across retries and enforce uniqueness in the database. A disabled button alone does not protect against duplicate server writes.
gap: Production reliability, offline queuing, intentional duplicate-receipt detection, and a long-term operation-key retention policy were not established.
handover: The handover retained the lost-response reproduction, database constraint description, payload-conflict rule, and regression checklist. A future team can adapt the submission pattern to another record-creation workflow. It must choose the correct actor scope and key lifetime for that workflow, rather than copying an expense-specific assumption or claiming that payment safety has been proven.

title: Supplier Onboarding Workspace
summary: Threadline Delivery built a workspace for checking supplier documents. It distinguished an incomplete checklist, a review in progress, and a supplier accepted for the client's directory.
problem: Purchasing staff collected supplier contact details and business documents in email threads. A filled form was sometimes mistaken for a completed review. The client needed a visible checklist with the identity of the person who checked each document. The software was intended to organize the client's own process, not certify a supplier or perform independent due diligence.
users: A coordinator created a supplier record and attached document references. A reviewer recorded whether required items were present and readable. A directory administrator accepted or declined the record for internal use. A supplier could appear in the directory only after the assigned review was complete. Directory acceptance did not authorize a purchase or verify bank-account ownership.
workflow: Records moved from collecting documents to under review and then accepted or declined. Missing items kept the checklist incomplete. Replacing a reviewed document invalidated that item's check and reopened review. The supplier directory showed both current review state and the version of the checklist used, so that a later change in required items could be explained.
constraints: The workspace used PostgreSQL records and private document storage. Reviewers could access only their assigned work queue. The pilot did not automate identity checks, risk scoring, bank validation, order placement, or payment authorization. Staff still made the acceptance decision, and external documents could be wrong even when the application successfully stored and displayed them.
decision: Document presence and supplier acceptance were stored as separate states. A required_document row described the item and checklist version, while document_check recorded reviewer, timestamp, source version, and result. The accept transition required completed checks for the active checklist. Upload success alone never set the supplier to accepted.
detail: The directory exposed a supplier identifier, display name, review state, and review version. Downstream tools were expected to look up the identifier rather than compare display names. Replacing a contact name did not create a new supplier identity. No interface in this pilot guaranteed that a directory entry was valid for a particular purchase amount or branch.
example: Supplier SUP-031 had a readable contact form but was missing one required attachment. Its record stayed in collecting documents. After the attachment arrived, a reviewer completed the remaining check and the administrator accepted the directory entry. A later replacement of that attachment reopened its check instead of inheriting the old review automatically.
test: Functional checks covered missing required items, acceptance with a completed checklist, document replacement, and an unassigned reviewer attempting a write. Acceptance was blocked until the required checks were complete. The checks used invented supplier records and local test files. They did not assess whether document contents were truthful or whether the supplier was commercially suitable.
result: The delivered workflow blocked directory acceptance while required document checks were incomplete and reopened the affected check after document replacement.
incident: The initial prototype labelled a completed upload as ready, which reviewers interpreted as ready for directory acceptance. The team replaced that label with documents uploaded and displayed review state separately. The handover explicitly warned downstream consumers not to treat an accepted supplier record as authority to approve a purchase or release money.
lesson: Separate document collection, human review, and business authorization. A complete checklist is evidence that a process ran, not proof that every downstream action is permitted.
gap: Bank validation, supplier risk assessment, and purchase authorization were outside the delivered scope. No reduction in onboarding effort was measured.
handover: The reusable material is a checklist definition, source-version review rule, and explicit state transition table. A future project must ask which supplier checks are required and who owns them. If a new brief says only purchasing, it should not silently grow supplier onboarding into the first release without confirming that requirement with the client.

title: Invoice Matching Pilot
summary: Threadline Delivery piloted invoice matching against purchase records. Unresolved matching errors caused the pilot to be stopped, and staff completed the cycle with the existing manual process.
problem: Accounts staff compared supplier invoices with purchase references and received-item records. A prototype tried to match on supplier display name and a normalized purchase reference. Several references were missing or reused, and similar supplier names made an apparently convenient matching rule unsafe. The client wanted less manual reconciliation, but that benefit remained a goal rather than an observed result.
users: An accounts operator imported invoice records and examined suggested matches. A reviewer checked unresolved items before any external posting process. A release owner could stop the pilot and return to the manual worksheet. The application generated a review queue only; it had no permission to post accounting entries or transfer funds automatically.
workflow: The proposed flow imported invoices, suggested a purchase match, compared recorded amounts, and required a reviewer to accept or reject the suggestion. Ambiguous or missing matches stayed unresolved. A complete batch required each invoice to be accounted for. The manual worksheet remained available while the pilot was tested, and reconciliation discrepancies prevented the pilot batch from being treated as complete.
constraints: The trial used a copied dataset and no live posting credentials. Supplier display names were not reliable identifiers. The client had not agreed a tolerance policy for differences in tax, freight, and partial deliveries. Those missing rules mattered to reconciliation. They could not safely be replaced by an arbitrary software threshold or hidden behind a single matched status.
decision: After reviewing the defects, the team required stable supplier identifiers, explicit purchase revisions, and a reason for every accepted exception. A batch could not advance while unresolved reconciliation items remained. These were corrective design decisions for a possible future iteration; they were not implemented and validated as a successful replacement pilot during this project.
detail: The trial retained imported invoice rows, suggested purchase IDs, review decisions, and reconciliation exceptions. The rollback did not delete these records. An exception recorded the unmatched invoice, conflicting candidate references, reason, and reviewer note. The manual process used the original invoice and purchase material rather than trusting a suggestion simply because it had a populated match field.
example: An invoice from a supplier's trading name resembled two directory names. The prototype chose the first candidate and attached a purchase with a reused reference. Review found that the invoice covered a different delivery. The match was withdrawn, the item remained unresolved, and the operator used the original documents in the manual reconciliation process.
test: The trial review deliberately included ambiguous supplier names, reused references, partial deliveries, and missing purchase records. Review found unresolved errors in the suggested matches. The team stopped the pilot before external posting. The notes do not record a repaired algorithm passing the same trial, so the review cannot be cited as proof of automated matching accuracy.
result: The invoice-matching pilot was stopped because unresolved matching errors remained. Staff completed the cycle manually; no automated posting was performed.
incident: A release note initially described the cycle as completed without distinguishing manual completion from success of the matching tool. The delivery review corrected that wording. The business cycle was completed through fallback, while the automation pilot failed its acceptance condition. Both facts are retained so that future teams do not copy an inaccurate success story.
lesson: Do not treat a populated match field or a completed manual fallback as proof that automation succeeded. Preserve unresolved exceptions and block dependent actions until the reconciliation rule is agreed.
gap: A repaired matching service, measured time savings, accepted tolerance rules, and production matching accuracy were not established.
handover: The retained material includes the exception examples, stop decision, manual fallback checklist, and proposed corrections. These documents can inform a release gate or a reconciliation discussion. They do not provide a validated matching engine. Any new project should keep approval and downstream posting separate instead of inferring that an approved request has already been ordered, received, or paid.

title: Branch Inventory Request Portal
summary: Threadline Delivery built a branch inventory request portal. Branch staff saw their own records, while explicitly assigned central reviewers could inspect requests across branches.
problem: Branch staff requested stock transfers using a shared spreadsheet. Filters were convenient for navigation but did not prevent someone from opening another branch's record. The client wanted clear branch ownership and a central review role. The project concerned internal stock-transfer requests, not purchasing new stock from suppliers or recording financial approval.
users: A branch requester belonged to an active branch assignment. A branch lead reviewed local requests. A central reviewer had an explicit cross-branch assignment. A support operator could investigate an access error without granting a requester central privileges. Staff with multiple branch assignments had to choose the branch for a new request rather than inheriting the last branch used by another screen.
workflow: The requester selected an assigned branch and submitted requested stock quantities. The server stored branch ownership on the request. List, detail, edit, and review operations all checked the active user assignment. Central review listed only records allowed by the central role. A browser-provided branch identifier was a requested scope, not evidence that the user had permission to use it.
constraints: The portal used existing sign-in and PostgreSQL. Branch assignment came from an administrator-maintained table. The first release did not synchronize assignments with a corporate directory or manage staff transfers automatically. The client also retained its stock ledger outside this application. An approved transfer request did not prove that a movement had physically occurred.
decision: Authorization was enforced in server-side record queries and writes, not only in the list screen. The server resolved branch membership from the signed-in employee and checked the target record's stored branch. A central review capability was separate from a branch requester's assignment. This prevented a user from changing a URL or request body to obtain a different branch's records.
detail: The data model used employee_assignment, branch, inventory_request, and review_event. An assignment had a role and active flag. The application checked assignments on each operation rather than storing a permanent branch entitlement in a browser form. A request retained its original branch identity after creation; changing the employee's current assignment did not silently move historical requests between branches.
example: A North Branch requester copied the URL of a South Branch request. The server returned access denied rather than relying on the North Branch list filter. A central reviewer with an explicit active assignment could read both records. When the North requester lost that assignment, subsequent edits were denied even if a browser tab had been left open.
test: Controlled checks covered direct-link access, a forged branch identifier, cross-branch editing, an inactive assignment, and an explicitly authorized central reviewer. The tested requester could not read or modify another branch's request. The checks used two fictional branches and test identities; they did not establish organization-wide identity governance or validate integration with a real directory.
result: The two-branch acceptance checks rejected unauthorized cross-branch reads and writes while allowing an explicitly assigned central reviewer to inspect both branches.
incident: The team found that an early detail endpoint checked sign-in but did not check the request's branch. The endpoint was corrected before pilot acceptance and tested independently of the list screen. The delivery review records the defect to make clear why a filtered interface was not an adequate permission boundary.
lesson: Check the actor's current assignment against the record's stored branch on every server read and write. A filtered list does not establish authorization.
gap: Automatic directory synchronization, staff-transfer policy, purchasing authority, and real stock movement were outside the pilot's evidence.
handover: The handover included an authorization matrix, endpoint checks, and examples of denied direct access. These are patterns and test cases rather than a complete identity integration. A future project must decide who assigns branch managers and finance reviewers, how assignments expire, and whether central staff may approve or only inspect records.

title: Audit Export Dashboard
summary: Threadline Delivery built an event-history export for internal reviewers. Each exported event identified its actor, server timestamp, action, record revision, and export scope.
problem: Reviewers could see a request's final state but could not reliably explain how it reached that state. A spreadsheet download sometimes changed while a reviewer paged through it, making row counts difficult to reconcile. The client needed a bounded event-history export and a visible statement of the filters and time range used to generate it.
users: A service operator performed normal request actions. An internal reviewer inspected events and requested exports. A system administrator managed access but did not rewrite application events through the dashboard. The export supported operational review. It was not described as a certified compliance record, a legally sufficient audit, or a cryptographically tamper-proof archive.
workflow: A successful request transition wrote an event in the same transaction. A reviewer chose an authorized record scope and date range, then requested an export. The system recorded a cutoff and produced rows up to that cutoff. The download header identified the filters, generation time, cutoff, and included record count so that a reviewer could explain the result's boundaries.
constraints: The pilot used PostgreSQL and CSV output. Timestamps were stored in UTC and the display timezone was labelled. Raw receipt attachments and secret tokens were excluded. The retention duration had not been approved by the client, so the application did not automatically delete old events. The project did not claim protection against a privileged database administrator changing stored data.
decision: Application users could append new events through normal state transitions but could not edit or delete earlier events through the dashboard. Corrections were new events referencing the earlier record. The team deliberately used append-only at the application layer rather than claiming that this design alone established immutable infrastructure or formal compliance.
detail: An event contained event_id, record_id, revision, actor_id, action, previous_state, next_state, and occurred_at. The export job also stored its requesting reviewer, scope, cutoff, and count. Access filtering applied before export. For text that began with spreadsheet formula characters, the CSV writer emitted a safe text representation so exported notes could not become active spreadsheet formulas.
example: A reviewer exported one team's request history through the recorded cutoff. A later approval created a new event but did not change the already generated file. A correction to a request reason appeared as a later correction event rather than rewriting the original event. Another team's records were absent because the reviewer did not have access to that scope.
test: Acceptance checks compared exported rows with the selected scope and cutoff, checked actor and revision fields, tested a later event, and opened hostile-looking cell text as text. These were functional checks of the pilot exporter. They did not assess external audit standards, disaster recovery, long-term retention, or privileged-administrator tampering.
result: The pilot export included the selected authorized events through its cutoff, with actor, timestamp, action, revision, and a recorded export scope.
incident: An early export queried live pages independently and could include a later event on one page while missing another event from an earlier page. The team changed the flow to use a recorded cutoff and a stable export ordering. The correction made the pilot download explainable, but it did not establish a general guarantee for every possible future export size.
lesson: Record event provenance and export boundaries. Preserve corrections as new events, and avoid describing an application event log as tamper-proof or compliant without separate evidence.
gap: Retention policy, legal compliance, privileged-administrator tamper resistance, and maximum export capacity were not established.
handover: The retained material is an event-field checklist, cutoff example, export permission check, and safe-cell test. A future team can use these to design an explainable request history. It still needs agreement on who may export, which sensitive fields are excluded, how long records are retained, and how large exports should be delivered.

title: Staff Leave Approval Tool
summary: Threadline Delivery built leave-request review with time-bounded manager delegation. It recorded the acting reviewer and the manager on whose behalf a decision was made.
problem: Leave requests waited when a manager was unavailable. Staff needed a named temporary reviewer instead of sharing manager credentials or treating an email reply as permanent permission. The team needed a way to explain who acted and why that person had authority at the time of the decision. This was a staffing workflow, with no financial spending limits.
users: An employee requested leave. Their manager could approve or reject it. An administrator could register a temporary delegate for a specified manager and period. The delegate could act only within that active assignment. The project did not decide staffing policy, approve payroll changes, or treat a delegate as a permanent replacement manager.
workflow: A leave request moved from submitted to reviewed. When a delegate reviewed it, the server checked the delegation at decision time and recorded both actor and represented manager. Expired delegation could not authorize another decision. A manager returning from leave could still inspect earlier decisions, with the original actor retained rather than rewritten as if the manager had clicked the button.
constraints: The pilot used existing staff identities and a manually maintained manager map. There was a single managerial review stage. Financial amount thresholds, separation of manager and finance duties, purchase revisions, and supplier records were outside scope. A colleague being an appropriate leave delegate did not establish that the same person could authorize spending.
decision: A delegation was an explicit record with principal manager, delegate, allowed action, start, and expiry. The server evaluated it when approving, rather than caching a permanent delegate flag in the browser. Approval history recorded the actual actor and the principal. A delegate could not create another delegation to an additional person.
detail: The request stored its assigned manager. A decision referenced either that manager acting directly or a valid delegation record. The UI displayed acting for only when a decision actually used delegation. After expiry, old decisions remained visible as history, but new writes required another current assignment. This separated historical explanation from current authority.
example: Manager M-03 delegated leave review to colleague D-02 for an agreed week. D-02 approved a leave request during that window, and the history retained both identities. A request sent after expiry could still be read by an otherwise authorized user, but D-02's attempted approval was denied unless a new delegation had been registered.
test: Controlled checks covered an active delegation, expiry before approval, a forged manager identifier, and an attempt to delegate onward. The correct acting and represented identities appeared in accepted decisions. The tests did not include financial limits, branch purchasing authority, or an automated organization-directory integration, and they did not measure employee scheduling outcomes.
result: The manager-delegation pilot accepted decisions within an active assignment, rejected expired authority, and retained the actual acting reviewer in history.
incident: An early interface showed only the principal manager's name in the history. Reviewers could not tell that a delegate had acted. The team corrected the display and decision record before handover. That correction improved traceability; it did not create a policy that delegation should be allowed in every approval workflow.
lesson: Represent delegated authority explicitly, evaluate it at decision time, and retain the actual actor. Do not infer spending authority from an unrelated managerial role.
gap: Financial authorization, purchasing delegation policy, directory synchronization, and staffing benefits were not established.
handover: The handover included an assignment example, expiry tests, and actor-display rules. A future client should first decide whether delegation is allowed and whether the delegate may perform the same action or only review it. The existence of this project is a reason to ask that question, not a reason to add delegation silently to another project's first release.

title: Marketing Content Approval Tool
summary: Threadline Delivery built an editorial approval tool for marketing drafts. It supported comments, review notifications, and publication scheduling; it did not authorize purchases or financial commitments.
problem: Editors exchanged campaign drafts through email and lost track of which comments needed a response. The client wanted a visible review queue and a notification when a draft needed attention. Content could continue changing during editorial review. The business intentionally preferred flexible collaboration over treating every text edit as a new financial authorization decision.
users: An author created a draft, a reviewer commented and marked it reviewed, and an editor scheduled publication. The reviewer role described editorial responsibility. It did not carry a spending limit or branch financial authority. The publishing editor remained responsible for checking the final copy, so a reviewed marker was not presented as an immutable approval of every later character.
workflow: Drafts moved through writing, in review, reviewed, and scheduled. Comments stayed attached to the draft, and notifications used a link back to the work item. The author could make copy edits during review. The review history recorded activity but did not freeze the exact text version or require an additional decision every time a comma or headline changed.
constraints: The application managed text and scheduling metadata, not invoices or purchase totals. It used a browser editor, server notifications, and PostgreSQL. It did not include approval thresholds, a manager-and-finance chain, branch assignment enforcement, or a financial event ledger. The review workflow should be assessed in its editorial context rather than treated as a generic authorization engine.
decision: The client chose editable drafts and lightweight review markers. A notification linked to the current draft, and the editor checked final text before scheduling. The team explicitly declined a revision-locked sign-off because that was not the agreed editorial workflow. This choice was suitable for the stated pilot but was never validated for authorization of money or goods.
detail: The model held content_draft, comment, review_marker, and notification. Notifications identified the work item and reason without including a complete draft in email. The current draft remained mutable; review_marker did not contain a complete approved text snapshot. Reviewer assignment was editorial and did not encode financial separation of duties or a purchase amount.
example: An author submitted a campaign headline, received a wording comment, and changed the copy while review was still open. The reviewer marked the draft reviewed, and the editor later adjusted punctuation before scheduling publication. The tool retained the activity, but it did not ask for another review after that final edit under the client's agreed workflow.
test: The pilot checks covered comment creation, a review-queue notification, access for assigned editors, and a scheduled item appearing in the editor's list. The team did not run tests for immutable approved amounts, duplicate purchase submission, two-stage financial review, or finance identity. Those guarantees cannot be inferred from successful editorial tests.
result: The editorial pilot delivered draft comments, review notifications, and scheduling status. It did not deliver revision-bound financial approval.
incident: One stakeholder used approved as shorthand for reviewed. During handover, the team clarified the label because it could be misunderstood as a locked final text. The product retained its flexible editorial behavior. A wording clarification should not be retold as delivery of a revision-controlled authorization feature that was never built.
lesson: A familiar approval label does not establish equivalent business authority. Reuse notification and work-queue ideas only after checking the new workflow's decision and revision requirements.
gap: Financial authorization, amount thresholds, immutable approved revisions, and purchasing outcomes were outside this project's scope.
handover: The team retained notification copy, review-queue states, and the discussion explaining mutable drafts. These are useful records of an editorial product. A new team should inspect them to understand both possible reuse and mismatch, instead of selecting this implementation solely because its title contains the word approval.

title: Purchasing Expansion Proposal
summary: Threadline Delivery proposed a purchasing expansion with amount-based finance review. The client paused the proposal before implementation, so it supplies design discussion but no delivered precedent or achieved outcome.
problem: After its one-office purchasing pilot, Meadow considered expansion to additional offices. The proposal described manager approval followed by finance review above a configurable threshold. The client had not agreed the threshold, finance assignment ownership, or handling of edits between stages. These were questions for discovery, not rules already operating in a delivered system.
users: The proposed users were office requesters, assigned managers, finance reviewers, and an administrator maintaining assignments. The proposal described responsibilities but did not provision real roles or grant authority. A person appearing in a design diagram was not evidence of an implemented permission check. The original one-office pilot remained the only delivered purchasing workflow in this client history.
workflow: The design sketch moved a submitted request to manager review and, where required by a future policy, then to finance review. It proposed binding both decisions to a single request revision. An edited amount would invalidate earlier decisions. The diagram contained unresolved branches for delegation, absence of a finance reviewer, and the meaning of a rejection at the second stage.
constraints: The document was a discovery proposal prepared before funding approval. No sprint was authorized, no migration was applied, and no acceptance environment was created. A four-week delivery estimate in an early email was explicitly labelled preliminary and contingent on policy decisions. It was not a record of completed work, a reliable estimate for a different client, or evidence of improved approval speed.
decision: The design discussion favored a versioned approval-policy definition rather than a hard-coded finance flag. A proposed decision record would identify policy version, stage, actor, and request revision. The note explains a possible approach and alternatives; none of the proposed tables or endpoints was implemented under this project. The original pilot's delivered behavior was not changed.
detail: Open design items included whether the threshold used a tax-inclusive total, whether a manager could also serve as finance reviewer, who maintained assignments, and how a policy change affected in-flight requests. The proposal suggested resolving these questions before implementing transition logic. There was no signed-off policy and no completed concurrency or authorization test to cite.
example: A workshop used a fictional request near an undecided threshold to discuss routing. Participants disagreed on whether a later amount edit should restart manager review or only finance review. The sketch proposed restarting both stages for a changed revision, but the workshop did not close the policy decision. The example was a design exercise rather than an executed application workflow.
test: The proposal listed future checks for threshold boundaries, edits after manager approval, missing finance assignments, and concurrent decisions. No checks were executed for this expansion. A list of intended tests must not be presented as passing results. The team retained the list so another discovery effort could evaluate it against that client's actual policy.
result: No implementation, acceptance test result, or production outcome was recorded for the purchasing expansion. The client paused the proposal before authorizing delivery.
incident: A handover index initially grouped the expansion beside completed projects. The archive owner added proposal only to the status and preserved the pause decision. The index correction did not change delivery history: the one-office pilot existed, while this later multi-stage expansion remained a proposal with unresolved requirements.
lesson: Treat an unimplemented proposal as an option to investigate, not a proven solution. Separate an intended workflow, a preliminary estimate, and an executed acceptance result.
gap: The finance threshold, policy ownership, implementation, test execution, delivery estimate, and business outcomes were not established for this proposal.
handover: The retained material consists of workshop questions, a design sketch, and an explicit paused status. A future project can use the questions to structure discovery, but should cite delivered work separately and validate the new design. No source code, finished multi-stage approval component, or measured benefit is provided by this proposal.
